Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

WASHINGTON (CNN) -- Investigators with bomb-making components in their luggage and on their person were able to pass through security checkpoints at 19 U.S. airports without detection, according to the Government Accountability Office. Passengers pass through security at O'Hare International Airport in Chicago, Illinois. GAO officials are expected to testify about the investigation Thursday before the House Committee on Oversight and Government Reform. The investigators reported that most of the time security officers followed Transportation Security Administration policies and procedures, but investigators were able to take advantage of "weaknesses in TSA procedures and other vulnerabilities." "These weaknesses were identified based on a review of public information," the planned GAO testimony says. Investigators concluded that if they had attempted the same test at other airports, they would have evaded detection. But the GAO did not detail the weaknesses because they "are sensitive security information." The investigators obtained the bomb-making components at local stores and over the Internet for less than $150, according to testimony.  Watch a tester point out a TSA mistake » . The GAO said its investigators also tested the devices that could be built with the components they smuggled and discovered that "a terrorist using these devices could cause severe damage to an airplane and threaten the safety of passengers." The GAO investigators devised two types of devices: an "improvised explosive device" made of a liquid explosive and a low-yield detonator, and an "improvised incendiary device" that could be created by combining commonly available products prohibited in carry-on luggage. The GAO said it found the instructions for creating the devices "using publicly available information," including Internet searches. According to the testimony, a transportation security officer barred one of the investigators from bringing an unlabeled bottle of medicated shampoo through the checkpoint. But the security officer allowed a liquid component of the improvised explosive device to pass through undetected, although that item is prohibited by the TSA. In another test, the investigator put coins in his pockets to assure he would get a secondary inspection. But the officer, using a hand-wand and a pat-down, failed to detect any of the prohibited items the investigator was carrying. The GAO said it had briefed the TSA on its findings "to help them take corrective action." In testimony to be provided to the same congressional committee, TSA chief Kip Hawley defends the administration's policies and procedures, saying that the screening checkpoints are but one of a "multilayered approach to security." "We recognize that, despite our efforts to make each layer as strong as possible, a concerted effort may target any one layer," according to the testimony. "Our ongoing success is a result of the tremendous power in the reinforced, multiple layers. Truly, the whole is greater than the sum of the parts -- and together, they are formidable." Hawley sketches for members of Congress 19 security steps the TSA employs before, during and after checkpoint screening. "Each and every one of these 19 security layers is important and strong in its own right," he says. "Linked together, they are effective and daunting." Although it would not discuss the specific nature of its recommendations, the GAO said it recommended establishing special screening lines based on risk and passengers with special needs. The TSA should introduce more "aggressive, visible and unpredictable" measures to detect concealed items and develop new technology for screening at checkpoints. Hawley's said the TSA concurs with the GAO's recommendations and specifically discussed several "new technology" items that he said were "greatly improving our effectiveness in detecting prohibited items." Among the new technology, he said, were whole body imagers, bottled liquids scanners, hand-held explosives scanners and advanced technology X-rays. And, he added, "our pursuit of new technology is not limited to what I described today." He also said the TSA is constantly conducting covert tests of the screening process, including detection of prohibited liquids and IEDs. "The nation's aviation system remains secure," he said, "but requires ongoing improvement and vigilance to stay ahead of the threat of terrorism."  E-mail to a friend .

WASHINGTON (CNN) — Investigators carrying bomb-making components in their luggage and on their person were able to pass through security checkpoints at 19 U.S. airports without detection, according to the Government Accountability Office.

Passengers pass through security at O’Hare International Airport in Chicago, Illinois.

GAO officials are expected to testify about the investigation Thursday before the House Committee on Oversight and Government Reform. Investigators reported that, in most instances, security officers followed Transportation Security Administration policies and procedures; however, the investigators were able to exploit “weaknesses in TSA procedures and other vulnerabilities.”

“These weaknesses were identified based on a review of public information,” the planned GAO testimony states.

Investigators concluded that, had they attempted the same test at other airports, they would have evaded detection. The GAO did not specify the weaknesses, however, because they “are sensitive security information.”

According to the testimony, investigators obtained the bomb-making components from local stores and over the Internet for less than $150. Watch a tester point out a TSA mistake »

The GAO said its investigators also tested devices that could be built with the smuggled components and found that “a terrorist using these devices could cause severe damage to an airplane and threaten the safety of passengers.”

GAO investigators devised two types of devices: an “improvised explosive device” made from a liquid explosive and a low-yield detonator, and an “improvised incendiary device” that could be created by combining commonly available products prohibited in carry-on luggage.

The GAO said it found instructions for creating the devices “using publicly available information,” including Internet searches.

According to the testimony, a transportation security officer prevented one investigator from bringing an unlabeled bottle of medicated shampoo through the checkpoint. However, the officer allowed a liquid component of the improvised explosive device to pass through undetected, even though the item is prohibited by the TSA.

In another test, an investigator placed coins in his pockets to ensure he would receive a secondary inspection. But the officer, using a hand wand and a pat-down, failed to detect any of the prohibited items the investigator was carrying.

The GAO said it had briefed the TSA on its findings “to help them take corrective action.”

In testimony to be provided to the same congressional committee, TSA chief Kip Hawley defends the agency’s policies and procedures, saying that screening checkpoints are only one element of a “multilayered approach to security.”

“We recognize that, despite our efforts to make each layer as strong as possible, a concerted effort may target any one layer,” the testimony says. “Our ongoing success is a result of the tremendous power in the reinforced, multiple layers. Truly, the whole is greater than the sum of the parts — and together, they are formidable.”

Hawley outlines for members of Congress 19 security measures the TSA employs before, during, and after checkpoint screening.

“Each and every one of these 19 security layers is important and strong in its own right,” he says. “Linked together, they are effective and daunting.”

Although it would not discuss the specific nature of its recommendations, the GAO said it recommended establishing special screening lines based on risk and for passengers with special needs. It also said the TSA should introduce more “aggressive, visible and unpredictable” measures to detect concealed items and develop new technology for checkpoint screening.

Hawley said the TSA concurs with the GAO’s recommendations and specifically discussed several “new technology” items that he said were “greatly improving our effectiveness in detecting prohibited items.”

Among the new technologies, he said, are whole-body imagers, bottled-liquids scanners, hand-held explosives scanners, and advanced-technology X-rays. He added, “Our pursuit of new technology is not limited to what I described today.”

He also said the TSA is constantly conducting covert tests of the screening process, including efforts to detect prohibited liquids and IEDs.

“The nation’s aviation system remains secure,” he said, “but requires ongoing improvement and vigilance to stay ahead of the threat of terrorism.”

WASHINGTON (CNN) — Government Accountability Office investigators carrying bomb-making materials in their bags and on their bodies successfully moved through security checkpoints at 19 airports across the United States without being stopped, the GAO said.

The findings were expected to be presented Thursday to the House Committee on Oversight and Government Reform. According to the GAO’s planned testimony, screeners generally complied with Transportation Security Administration rules and procedures, but the investigators still managed to exploit “weaknesses in TSA procedures and other vulnerabilities.”

The GAO said those weaknesses were discovered through a review of publicly available information. Investigators also determined that, had they conducted the same operation at additional airports, they likely would have avoided detection there as well. The agency did not describe the specific shortcomings, saying they constitute “sensitive security information.”

The components used in the tests were purchased from local retailers and online for under $150, the testimony said. The GAO also tested devices that could be assembled from the smuggled materials and found that “a terrorist using these devices could cause severe damage to an airplane and threaten the safety of passengers.”

Investigators designed two categories of devices: an improvised explosive device using a liquid explosive and a low-yield detonator, and an improvised incendiary device made by mixing common consumer products that are banned from carry-on bags. The GAO said directions for making the devices were found through public sources, including Internet searches.

In one case, a transportation security officer stopped an investigator from taking an unlabeled bottle of medicated shampoo through a checkpoint. However, the same officer did not detect a liquid ingredient for the improvised explosive device, even though the TSA prohibits that item.

In another trial, an investigator deliberately placed coins in his pockets so he would be sent for additional screening. Even after using a hand-held wand and conducting a pat-down, the officer failed to find any of the banned items the investigator had with him.

The GAO said it had already informed the TSA of its conclusions so the agency could begin corrective steps.

In separate testimony prepared for the same House committee, TSA Administrator Kip Hawley defended the agency’s practices, saying airport checkpoints are only one element of a broader “multilayered approach to security.”

“We recognize that, despite our efforts to make each layer as strong as possible, a concerted effort may target any one layer,” Hawley’s testimony said. “Our ongoing success is a result of the tremendous power in the reinforced, multiple layers. Truly, the whole is greater than the sum of the parts — and together, they are formidable.”

Hawley outlined 19 TSA security measures used before, during and after checkpoint screening. “Each and every one of these 19 security layers is important and strong in its own right,” he said. “Linked together, they are effective and daunting.”

While the GAO declined to disclose the details of its recommendations, it said it urged the creation of dedicated screening lanes based on passenger risk and the needs of travelers requiring special assistance. It also recommended that TSA adopt more “aggressive, visible and unpredictable” methods for finding hidden items and continue developing new checkpoint-screening technology.

Hawley said the TSA agreed with the GAO’s recommendations and pointed to several new technologies that he said were “greatly improving our effectiveness in detecting prohibited items.” Those included whole-body imaging machines, scanners for bottled liquids, hand-held explosives detectors and advanced X-ray systems.

“Our pursuit of new technology is not limited to what I described today,” he added.

Hawley also said the TSA routinely carries out undercover tests of its screening system, including efforts focused on banned liquids and improvised explosive devices.

“The nation’s aviation system remains secure,” he said, “but requires ongoing improvement and vigilance to stay ahead of the threat of terrorism.”

counterfactuals.output:
**GAO report: Undercover testers carried simulated bomb parts through security at 19 U.S. airports without detection**

*By Staff Writer*  
*Washington —*

Undercover government investigators were able to carry components for simulated explosive devices through passenger security checkpoints at 19 airports across the United States without being stopped, according to findings from a Government Accountability Office review that is raising new concerns about aviation security screening.

The GAO investigation, conducted at the request of lawmakers, found that covert testers repeatedly passed through airport checkpoints with materials intended to represent bomb-making components. The items were not detected by screeners, according to officials familiar with the review.

The findings do not indicate that actual explosives were brought onto aircraft. Rather, the tests were designed to assess whether airport screening procedures and personnel could identify suspicious items and prevent prohibited materials from passing beyond the checkpoint.

Still, lawmakers said the results point to serious vulnerabilities in the nation’s aviation security system.

“This is exactly the kind of failure that keeps security experts up at night,” one congressional official said. “If trained testers can repeatedly get through checkpoints undetected, then TSA needs to explain what went wrong and how it will be fixed.”

The Transportation Security Administration, which oversees passenger screening at U.S. airports, said in a statement that it takes covert testing seriously and uses such results to improve training, technology and procedures.

“TSA continuously evaluates and updates its security protocols to address evolving threats,” the agency said. “Covert testing is an important tool for identifying gaps and strengthening checkpoint operations.”

The GAO’s findings come amid ongoing scrutiny of airport screening performance, including the effectiveness of checkpoint equipment, screener training and procedures for identifying concealed threats. Aviation security experts say the challenge is complicated by the high volume of travelers, the need to move passengers efficiently and the constantly changing tactics used by those who may seek to evade detection.

The report did not publicly identify the airports involved, citing security concerns. Officials said releasing detailed information about the tests could reveal weaknesses in screening procedures.

Members of Congress are expected to press TSA leaders for answers at upcoming oversight hearings, including whether additional training, updated technology or changes in checkpoint procedures are needed.

The GAO recommended that TSA review the failures identified during the undercover tests and take corrective action to ensure screeners can better detect prohibited and suspicious materials.

Security specialists said the results should be viewed as a warning rather than evidence of an immediate threat.

“Covert tests are meant to find weaknesses before an adversary does,” one former aviation security official said. “The key question now is whether the agency acts quickly and effectively on what the testing revealed.”

TSA said it has already begun reviewing the findings and will work with federal partners to address any identified vulnerabilities.

**WASHINGTON (CNN) — November 15, 2007** — Undercover government investigators were able to expose serious weaknesses in airport passenger-screening procedures, according to findings disclosed Thursday, raising new questions about the Transportation Security Administration’s ability to detect potentially dangerous items at checkpoints.

The investigators, working for the Government Accountability Office, posed as ordinary passengers and carried components that could be used to assemble an improvised explosive device through airport security screening. The tests were conducted at several U.S. airports as part of a review of TSA procedures and technology.

According to officials familiar with the findings, the undercover teams were able to pass through checkpoints without screeners identifying all of the suspicious materials. The results suggested that gaps remained in how carry-on bags were searched, how screeners interpreted X-ray images and how consistently procedures were applied across airports.

TSA Administrator Kip Hawley said the agency takes the results seriously but cautioned that covert testing is designed to find vulnerabilities.

“These tests are intentionally difficult, and they help us improve,” Hawley said in response to the findings. He said TSA had already made changes to training, checkpoint procedures and explosives-detection efforts, and would continue to use covert testing to strengthen security.

Hawley also emphasized that airport security is built in layers, including passenger vetting, behavior detection, canine teams, air marshals and law-enforcement presence, in addition to checkpoint screening.

“No single measure is perfect,” Hawley said. “The goal is to make the system stronger as a whole.”

Members of Congress said the findings were troubling, particularly years after the September 11 attacks led to the creation of TSA and a federal takeover of airport screening.

Lawmakers called for more aggressive oversight, improved screener training and faster deployment of advanced detection equipment capable of identifying explosives and other threats more reliably.

The report adds to long-running concerns about TSA’s performance in undercover tests. Previous audits have also found that screeners sometimes failed to detect weapons or simulated explosives, prompting repeated revisions to procedures and training programs.

TSA officials said passengers should not expect immediate visible changes at checkpoints but may see more random screening, additional bag checks and continued adjustments to prohibited-items enforcement as the agency responds to the latest findings.

**GAO investigators bypass TSA screening at 19 airports in covert test**

Government investigators were able to carry components for improvised explosive and incendiary devices through Transportation Security Administration checkpoints at 19 U.S. airports during covert testing, according to findings by the Government Accountability Office.

The tests, conducted to assess the effectiveness of airport passenger screening, found that GAO investigators repeatedly passed through security with prohibited materials despite TSA procedures designed to detect threats before passengers reach aircraft. The GAO said the results raised concerns about vulnerabilities in checkpoint screening and the need for continued improvements in screener training, technology and oversight.

The investigators did not assemble or use any device during the tests, and the GAO did not publicly disclose technical details that could aid an attack. The agency said its work was intended to evaluate whether TSA systems could identify dangerous components when carried by passengers.

TSA has long maintained that checkpoint screening is only one part of aviation security. The agency describes its approach as a “multilayered” defense designed to reduce risk through overlapping measures before and after passengers arrive at the airport.

Those layers include intelligence gathering and watch-list matching, travel-document verification, passenger and baggage screening, explosive-detection technologies, canine teams, behavior-detection efforts, random security measures, federal air marshals, armed pilots, hardened cockpit doors, crew training and public vigilance.

TSA officials have argued that because no single layer is foolproof, the system is designed so that if one measure fails, others may still prevent an attack. The agency has also said it continually updates screening procedures and equipment in response to emerging threats and findings from internal and external testing.

The GAO’s findings nevertheless underscore the challenge TSA faces in detecting concealed threats while processing large volumes of travelers. Lawmakers and security watchdogs have repeatedly pressed the agency to strengthen covert testing programs, improve screener performance and ensure that new technologies are deployed effectively.

The report adds to a long-running debate over how to balance speed, privacy and security at airport checkpoints while maintaining defenses against evolving aviation threats.
